fieldChanges.before: Calendar sharing sets a person’s baseline: Google’s levels are “See only free/busy (hide details)”, “See all event details”, “Make changes (see private events as free/busy)”, “Make changes and see event details” and “Make changes and manage sharing”. Event visibility then adjusts that baseline for one event: Default visibility, Public or Private.
fieldChanges.after: Calendar sharing sets a person’s baseline: Google’s levels are “See only free/busy (hide details)”, “See event details”, “Make changes (see private events as free/busy)”, “Make changes and see event details” and “Make changes and manage sharing”. Event visibility then adjusts that baseline for one event: Default visibility, Public or Private.

fieldChanges.before: What the others see depends on the event’s availability. Google states that a private event marked Busy appears as a busy block with no details, and a private event marked Free does not appear on your calendar at all for them.
fieldChanges.after: Google explicitly describes an additional distinction for the “Make changes (see private events as free/busy)” permission: a private item marked Busy appears as a busy block, while a private item marked Free is hidden from that recipient’s calendar grid. Do not generalise that exact display rule to every other permission level without checking the recipient’s view. Private controls details; Busy or Free separately describes availability.

fieldChanges.before: Private is about people viewing your calendar. Google notes that when you invite someone to an event, they control how it shows on their own calendar. Guests of a private event still receive its details through the invitation.
fieldChanges.after: An invitation and a calendar-sharing grant are separate routes. Private does not recall information already sent in an invitation. Google warns that some details can remain visible when guests or rooms are involved, including the event’s start, end and creator. Check the actual audience rather than treating Private as a confidentiality guarantee.

fieldChanges.before: A fictional manager adds “Contract renewal — Northwind, Room 4” on Thursday at 14:00 and marks it Private and Busy. Their calendar is shared four ways: a team Google Group with free/busy only, a peer with See all event details, an assistant with Make changes (see private events as free/busy), and a deputy with Make changes and see event details.
fieldChanges.after: A fictional manager adds “Contract renewal — Northwind, Room 4” on Thursday at 14:00 and marks it Private and Busy. Their calendar is shared four ways: a team Google Group with free/busy only, a peer with See event details, an assistant with Make changes (see private events as free/busy), and a deputy with Make changes and see event details.

fieldChanges.before: The group, the peer and the assistant each see a busy block at 14:00 with no title. The deputy sees the full entry. If the manager had marked it Private and Free, the first three would see nothing at all at 14:00 and might book over it. If it had been marked Public, all four would see the title and room.
fieldChanges.after: The group, the peer and the restricted editor each see a busy block at 14:00 without the private title; the deputy can read the details. For the restricted editor specifically, Google says changing that private event to Free hides it from their grid. Do not assume all other viewers have the same Free display. If this otherwise non-private event were marked Public, everyone with calendar-view access could read its details.

before: Open the event, choose edit, find the visibility control (shown as Default visibility until changed), pick Default visibility, Public or Private, and save. For tasks, Google says only tasks with a start and end time can have their visibility changed; tasks without times are always private.

To verify without exposing real data, ask a colleague who holds a known permission level to look at a harmless test event you mark Private and Busy, then Public. Do not share your account credentials to “see what they see”. On a work or school account, Google notes your administrator can limit sharing or turn off permission settings, so the levels you see may be fewer.
after: Open the event, choose edit, find the visibility control (shown as Default visibility until changed), pick Default visibility, Public or Private, and save. For tasks, Google says only tasks with a start and end time can have their visibility changed; tasks without times are always private.

To verify without exposing real data, ask a colleague who holds a known permission level to look at a harmless test event you mark Private and Busy, then Public. Do not share your account credentials to “see what they see”. On a work or school account, Google notes your administrator can limit sharing or turn off permission settings, so the levels you see may be fewer.

Recurring events have an important limit: Google documents one visibility setting for the whole series. Trying to change one occurrence or a subset applies the visibility change to the entire series. Use a harmless non-recurring event for the recipient-side test above.

This diagnostic concerns Google appointment schedules; Arte Soft develops Cloud Calendars and does not run Google’s booking pages.

fieldChanges.before: For work or school accounts, the new owner must be in the same organisation. Google also says events with more than 200 guests cannot be transferred to another owner or calendar. Moving an event between your own calendars is a different action and does not change the organiser.
fieldChanges.after: Google says events with more than 200 guests cannot be transferred to another owner or calendar. Its same-organisation requirement is stated under whole-calendar ownership transfer, not the separate event Change owner procedure. For an individual event, inspect the actual Change owner options and your organisation’s policy; this guide does not promise that every proposed recipient is eligible. Moving an event between calendars and changing its owner are separate operations.

fieldChanges.before: The check-in and review can be transferred to the incoming coordinator, who is in the same organisation. Before transferring the review, the coordinator asks whether the new owner’s account can record Meet calls; if not, recording will not be available after acceptance. fieldChanges.after: The coordinator checks the actual Change owner options for the check-in and review and confirms the intended recipient before sending. Before the review’s transfer, they ask whether the successor’s account supports Meet recording. The 240-guest all-hands exceeds Google’s documented transfer limit, so they coordinate a supported replacement owned by the successor and inform attendees how the original will be retired. A recurring meeting needs deliberate future-occurrence scope and preservation of useful history; do not delete an entire historical series as a handoff shortcut.

fieldChanges.before: The coordinator sends the transfers at least a week before leaving, then checks daily until each is accepted. On acceptance they open each event and confirm that it shows the new organiser.
fieldChanges.after: For illustration, the coordinator starts a week before leaving and follows up on pending requests. That is a planning example, not a required or sufficient lead time. Completion depends on the recipient actually accepting; afterwards, inspect the saved event’s organiser and required Meet features before closing the old account.

after: On a computer, choose Create, then Event, add guests and open Find a time. Google documents availability comparison for up to 50 guests; beyond that, only 50 schedules are shown. Filter and view lets you choose No guests, Required guests or All guests and show or hide rooms.

The key condition is Google’s own: these guests must have shared their calendars with you. If a person does not share their calendar with you, Google says you can send them a request to share it. Rooms are added with Add rooms or Add room booking.

A separate workflow puts subscribed calendars in dedicated columns in the main calendar grid: Settings > View options > View calendars side by side in Day View, then use Day view. That persistent subscribed-calendar setting is not a Find a time control.

fieldChanges.after: Private details and Free time. The event’s privacy, availability and your permission affect what is visible. Google explicitly documents hidden Private, Free items for the restricted-editor permission. A blank column does not reveal whether an unseen private appointment exists, and that role-specific display rule should not be projected onto every viewer.

fieldChanges.before: When you choose Delegate, Microsoft lets you decide where meeting requests and responses go: to your delegates only, to your delegates with a copy to you, or to both you and your delegates. Pick deliberately. If requests go only to the delegate, you will not see new invitations arrive yourself.
fieldChanges.after: Under Send invitations and responses to, Microsoft lists three choices. Delegate only sends requests and responses to delegates. Delegate and send me a copy sends both a copy, but the owner’s copy is a normal email without Accept/Decline controls there; the owner can still respond by opening the calendar item. Both my delegate and me gives both people actionable invitations. Agree who processes each request to avoid conflicting actions.

before: Microsoft’s delegate overview describes three per-folder levels. Reviewer can read items. Author can read and create items and change or delete items they created. Editor can do everything an Author can and also change and delete items you created.
Author is a sensible middle ground for someone who adds holds to your calendar but should not touch meetings you set up. Editor is needed when they must rework your existing entries.
after: Microsoft’s delegate overview describes three per-folder levels. Reviewer can read items. Author can read and create items and change or delete items they created. Editor can do everything an Author can and also change and delete items you created.
Author is a sensible middle ground for someone who adds holds to your calendar but should not touch meetings you set up. Editor is needed when they must rework your existing entries.

Do not treat the classic Private flag as a universal security boundary. Microsoft’s classic Outlook instructions explicitly warn against relying on it to prevent access when folder-read permissions such as Reviewer are granted. The classic checkbox is called Delegate can see my private items and can affect several Exchange folders; that is not the same scope as the new Outlook/web calendar checkbox.

fieldChanges.before: Check: the assistant accepts the sharing invitation, which Microsoft says adds the director’s calendar to their list. The director sends a test invitation from a colleague and confirms it reaches both inboxes as chosen.
fieldChanges.after: For a harmless test, ask a consenting colleague to send an invitation to the director. The assistant first accepts the calendar-sharing invitation. Then check the director’s normal-email copy and the assistant’s actionable request according to the selected routing option, rather than expecting identical buttons in both inboxes.

fieldChanges.before: In Outlook, someone who can change your calendar is not necessarily someone who handles your meetings. Microsoft separates the two, and the extra delegate options decide whether your invitations go to you, to them, or to both. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, wrote this guide to the owner’s side of that decision.
fieldChanges.after: This guide concerns Microsoft 365 or Exchange work-or-school calendars, mainly in new Outlook and Outlook on the web. Can edit and Delegate do different jobs, and invitation routing has separate consequences. Personal Outlook.com sharing and classic folder permissions are distinct cases. Arte Soft develops Cloud Calendars.

fieldChanges.after: That makes the practical recovery for a mis-filed meeting blunt: cancel it from the calendar where it was saved, then create it again on the correct calendar and tell the attendees why they received a cancellation and a new invitation. fieldChanges.before: A fictional account manager has “Pricing review — Contoso — Room 3B, 14:00–15:00” on Thursday, not marked Private. A colleague with Can view when I’m busy sees that 14:00–15:00 is busy. A colleague with Can view titles and locations sees “Pricing review — Contoso” and “Room 3B” but not the notes or attachments. A colleague with Can view all details sees everything in the entry.
fieldChanges.after: A fictional account manager has a non-private entry, “Pricing review — Contoso — Room 3B, 14:00–15:00”. A colleague with Can view when I’m busy sees the busy interval. Can view titles and locations reveals the title and room but not the appointment’s other fields. Can view all details reveals the calendar event’s available details; it does not establish permission to open a separately protected linked document or file.

fieldChanges.before: Microsoft recommends the simplified levels over custom permissions. Intermediate permissions set with PowerShell show as Custom, and Microsoft states custom levels are not supported in the newer sharing model. If you see Custom, ask your administrator before assuming what it allows.
fieldChanges.after: Microsoft’s newer sharing model displays simplified permission levels. Intermediate levels can still be configured by an administrator using mailbox-folder permission commands and appear as Custom. Client interfaces may allow an attempted action that the service then rejects; the service evaluates the underlying rights. Ask the administrator what the effective grant allows rather than treating every Custom level as unsupported.

fieldChanges.before: In Microsoft’s newer model, a copy of your shared calendar is created in the recipient’s mailbox and changes sync to it promptly in supported apps, which Microsoft lists as Outlook for Windows, Mac, web, iOS and Android, plus REST and Exchange ActiveSync apps; Exchange Web Services is excluded. After an upgrade, Microsoft says the copy includes events from one year before the upgrade date and all future events.
fieldChanges.after: In the newer Exchange Online model, a copy of the shared calendar is held in the recipient’s mailbox. Instant syncing is supported for specified configurations, including users within the same Microsoft 365 tenant, and supported Outlook, REST and Exchange ActiveSync applications. It is not universal for cross-tenant sharing. Microsoft says EWS does not support instant syncing; that is not a statement that EWS cannot access calendars at all. After an automatic upgrade, the copy includes the previous year and future events, including recurring series with relevant instances.

fieldChanges.before: Avoid custom permissions; ask an administrator if you see Custom.
fieldChanges.after: If a grant appears as Custom, ask the administrator what the actual permission permits; clients and the service may handle attempted actions differently.

fieldChanges.before: Microsoft also notes that sharing may be unavailable for your account or limited to your organisation depending on organisation settings. A missing option is usually layer one, not a fault in your mailbox.
fieldChanges.after: Microsoft notes that sharing can be unavailable or limited by organisation settings. A missing option is a reason to check the account, policy and intended recipient route with IT; it is not proof of one disabled switch or a broken mailbox.

fieldChanges.before: Microsoft says that when you share with someone outside the organisation, an Internet Calendar Subscription (ICS) URL is generated, which they can add to any calendar service. Microsoft gives typical refresh behaviour of approximately every three hours, and potentially every 24–48 hours depending on the recipient’s service.
fieldChanges.after: Outside the organisation does not always mean an ICS subscription. Microsoft distinguishes Microsoft 365-to-Microsoft 365 sharing between tenants with external sharing enabled: a full shared calendar is created and syncs periodically, approximately every three hours in the documented configuration. If external sharing is disabled, that other-tenant Microsoft 365 recipient falls into the ICS route instead.

fieldChanges.before: That means an external partner can be a day behind your changes through no fault of yours. For time-sensitive changes, tell them directly. Publishing a calendar as HTML or ICS from calendar settings is a separate, read-only route, and should not be used to work around a blocked share.
fieldChanges.after: Microsoft 365 sharing to Outlook.com or to a third-party service such as Gmail uses an ICS route. The recipient’s service decides when to refresh it. Microsoft gives Outlook.com at approximately three hours and Gmail at a possible 24–48 hours as service examples, not a universal maximum or delivery deadline. Confirm urgent changes directly. Publishing an HTML or ICS link is a separate read-only route and must not be used to bypass an organisation’s restrictions.

fieldChanges.before: If the share option for the designer’s address is missing entirely, the lead asks IT whether external sharing and email-invitation access are enabled. If the designer reports that a review moved yesterday still shows the old time, the lead checks their own calendar, then explains that the designer’s calendar app refreshes the subscription on its own schedule and confirms the new time by message.
fieldChanges.after: If the external share option is unavailable, the lead asks IT to check the account, external-sharing policy and intended recipient route. If the designer sees stale information, they first identify the actual calendar service and whether the share uses a cross-tenant calendar or an ICS subscription, then compare the source and confirm the important time by message. No fixed refresh deadline is assumed.

before: In classic Outlook or new Outlook for Windows, right-click the item on your calendar, choose Show As, then the status. Do this for entries that should not block bookings, such as a reminder to submit expenses, which would otherwise default to Busy.

In the Scheduling Assistant, Microsoft says busy time shows in dark blue, tentative appointments as a light blue hashed block, and time outside attendees’ working hours in light grey. That is how a colleague will read your choice.
after: In classic Outlook or new Outlook for Windows, right-click the item on your calendar, choose Show As, then the status. Do this for entries that should not block bookings, such as a reminder to submit expenses, which would otherwise default to Busy.

Read the status name and pattern in your actual client rather than relying on a universal colour. Microsoft’s Scheduling Assistant guidance illustrates busy and tentative with blue patterns, while its new Outlook availability page says Busy, Tentative and Working elsewhere colours adjust to the chosen calendar colour. A different palette is not itself evidence of a different availability state.

In new Outlook, changing an item’s availability after the initial invitation changes your calendar only. Microsoft says the organiser cannot rewrite every participant’s availability after that first invitation; attendees can customise their own. Verify the owner’s actual free/busy result rather than expecting your Show As edit to change everyone.

fieldChanges.before: A fictional consultant marks Monday’s client workshop Busy. Tuesday they work from a partner’s site, so they add an all-day item marked Working elsewhere: colleagues can still contact them but should not book an in-office room. Wednesday’s “Maybe join the vendor demo” is Tentative. A Thursday lunchtime reminder to call the bank is Free so it does not block bookings.
fieldChanges.after: A fictional consultant marks Monday’s client workshop Busy. Tuesday they add a Working elsewhere label for a day at a partner’s site. That communicates a location category; it does not enforce room-booking rules or establish whether another booking system treats it as unavailable. Wednesday’s optional vendor demo is Tentative. A Thursday lunchtime personal reminder is Free because it should not protect a meeting slot.

fieldChanges.before: Friday and the following Monday are leave. They do not tick “Decline and cancel my meetings” because a recurring team meeting they organise should still go ahead without them.
fieldChanges.after: For leave from the start of Friday through the end of the following Monday, including the weekend, the consultant chooses an explicit automatic-reply time interval. They select Block my calendar for this period and Automatically decline new invitations. They leave Decline and cancel my meetings unticked because a recurring team meeting they organise should continue without them.

fieldChanges.before: As organiser, open Response Options while creating or editing the meeting and clear Allow forwarding. Microsoft says forwarding is allowed by default. Attendees then do not get the forward option.
fieldChanges.after: As organiser, open Response Options while creating or editing the meeting and clear Allow forwarding. Microsoft says forwarding is allowed by default. Attendees then do not get the forward option. Microsoft limits the organiser’s feature to mailboxes hosted in Microsoft 365 or Exchange Server 2019; check mailbox eligibility as well as the client.

before: Microsoft is explicit that even with forwarding prevented, attendees can still reply or reply all to the invitation with an email message, and copy the meeting message or event. When an attendee uses an older client against an older Exchange version or a third-party service, the forward is handled by servers that do not support the feature, so it cannot be prevented.

Treat Allow forwarding as a guard against casual additions, not as access control. Keep sensitive material out of the invitation body and share documents with named people through their own permissions.
after: Microsoft is explicit that even with forwarding prevented, attendees can still reply or reply all to the invitation with an email message, and copy the meeting message or event. When an attendee uses an older client against an older Exchange version or a third-party service, the forward is handled by servers that do not support the feature, so it cannot be prevented.

Treat Allow forwarding as a guard against casual additions, not as access control. Keep sensitive material out of the invitation body and share documents with named people through their own permissions.

An older attendee client is not enough to establish a bypass. Microsoft says Exchange Online, Exchange 2016 and Exchange 2019 can reject a forwarding attempt even if an older client displays the command. Receiving and enforcing a restriction on mobile is also different from offering the organiser’s setting there.

fieldChanges.before: Microsoft states that by default, meeting invitations are not sent to every member’s inbox in the group. To invite them, add the group to the attendees list; new Outlook also offers an Invite members button. Microsoft says you, as creator, are automatically added as an attendee and the event appears on your personal calendar.
fieldChanges.after: In new Outlook, Outlook on the web and Outlook.com, Microsoft says creating a group-calendar event does not invite every member by default. Add the group to attendees when an invitation is intended; new Outlook also offers Invite members. The creator is automatically added as an attendee and receives the group event on their personal calendar in these documented flows.

fieldChanges.before: So an event can sit on the group calendar without appearing on members’ personal calendars or prompting a reply. If attendance matters, invite the group explicitly.
fieldChanges.after: Classic Outlook is different: Microsoft says the group alias is already in Required attendees when you create the group meeting. Remove the group if you do not intend invitations to its members. Whichever client you use, inspect the actual attendee list before sending rather than relying on one universal default.

fieldChanges.before: Invitations are not automatic
fieldChanges.after: Inspect invitations: the default differs by client

fieldChanges.before: Deadlines and on-site days go on the group calendar; members are not invited to each item, which avoids six inbox requests for every deadline. Client walkthroughs go on the lead’s own calendar with the client and relevant staff invited, and the lead shares that calendar with the team at Can view titles and locations.
fieldChanges.after: Deadlines and on-site days go on the group calendar. Before saving, the creator makes sure the group is not in the attendee list when no invitations are intended; in classic Outlook that can require removing the pre-populated group alias. Client walkthroughs go on the lead’s own calendar with the client and relevant staff invited. The team gets Can view titles and locations on that calendar, not editing or delegation rights.

fieldChanges.before: Microsoft says invitations are not sent to every member by default. Add the group to the attendees list.
